Begin work-up by ruling out pregnancy. It is also important to rule out medication side effects and hypothyroidism. A
If prolactinoma is found, treat medically, unless vision is imminently threatened. C
Bone loss may result from prolonged hyperprolactinemia. C

background.definition: Hyperprolactinemia, defined as elevated plasma levels of prolactin, is strictly a laboratory diagnosis. It may or may not be symptomatic. Macroprolactinemia, which is accumulation of biologically inactive large prolactin molecules, was reported in 22% to 42% of patients with hyperprolactinemia.

list.listitem: Hyperprolactinemia is more common in women, with an overall prevalence of 0.4%.
The prevalence is 9% to 17% in women with reproductive problems, including polycystic ovarian syndrome.
Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia occurs in 38% of psychiatric populations, with a female to male ratio of 2:1.
The most important effect of untreated hyperprolactinemia is hypogonadism. If hyperprolactinemia remains untreated, significant bone loss may result.
The etiologies of hyperprolactinemia () can be physiological, pharmacological, or pathological.
Physiological causes include pregnancy, lactation, nipple stimulation, and others.
Pharmacological causes include antipsychotics, antiemetics, antidepressants, estrogens, and less commonly central α-blockers and others.

Pathological causes: most common are pituitary tumors (mainly prolactinomas); also hypothalamic/pituitary stalk diseases (eg, compression by tumors, trauma to stalk, empty sella) and other less common causes.
A prolactinoma > 40 mm in diameter with prolactin level > 1000 ng/ml is commonly classified as a "giant prolactinoma".
Prolactin secretion is pulsatile, with diurnal variation, and is under the inhibitory control of dopamine.
Thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates prolactin secretion. Therefore, primary hypothyroidism (in which the TRH level is elevated) is associated with hyperprolactinemia.
Interruption of the hypothalamic connection (eg, stalk compression) results in prolactin oversecretion rather than undersecretion; that is, inhibition of the inhibitory effect of dopamine.
Hyperprolactinemia suppresses gonadotropin secretion in both sexes, resulting in hypogonadism.
Suspect hyperprolactinemia in females with amenorrhea, decreased libido or infertility, and in males with hypogonadism. The diagnosis is confirmed by laboratory testing. C
Before pursuing an extensive work-up for hyperprolactinemia, exclude pregnancy (in any woman of child-bearing age), medication side effect, and hypothyroidism. C
Exclude macroprolactinemia in asymptomatic or mild cases of hyperprolactinemia. B
Pregnancy is the major physiological cause of hyperprolactinemia.
Taking an extensive medication history is prudent to rule out iatrogenic hyperprolactinemia.

Although hyperprolactinemia may be asymptomatic, symptoms include galactorrhea (rare in men), amenorrhea or irregular menstruation, decreased libido, and infertility. Bone loss may result from prolonged hyperprolactinemia.
On physical examination, confirm the presence of galactorrhea (usually bilateral). In unilateral galactorrhea, consider discharge from anatomical lesions (eg, breast cancer).
When hyperprolactinemia is due to a hypothalamic/pituitary disease, other clinical features may be present according to the specific pathology.

When pituitary tumors are suspected, perform a meticulous visual examination, especially peripheral field testing and a fundus examination. Increasing tumor size is associated with a greater likelihood of abnormal visual field testing.

The normal range of prolactin may vary across laboratories; conventional units are ng/mL. Normal ranges (in ng/mL): In women: nonpregnant (2.8-29.2); pregnant (9.7-208.5); postmenopausal (1.8-20.3). In men: (2.1-17.7). For conversion to SI units (pmol/L), multiply by 43.5.

Prolactin secretion is pulsatile, and stimuli such as prior nipple stimulation may elevate prolactin levels transiently. Therefore, repeated testing is recommended. In a study of 95 patients with prolactinoma and 212 with non-functioning pituitary adenoma, a cutoff of 39 ng/ml was 99% sensitive but only 81% specific for distinguishing the two. The false positive rate was 19%, and the authors advised sequential imaging for patients with "borderline" results.
Order a pregnancy test and TSH level to rule out pregnancy and hypothyroidism.
If hyperprolactinemia is asymptomatic or mild, macroprolactinemia should be excluded by polyethylene glycol precipitation.
Prolactin levels correlate well with the size of prolactinomas, but not with other types of pituitary tumors. Prolactin levels higher than 250 ng/mL are almost always due to prolactinomas.

If a pituitary tumor is confirmed, appropriate tests for pituitary functions should be performed. These include pituitary and peripheral gland hormones to see if the tumor is functioning and to see if a deficiency state is present (eg, partial or panhypopituitarism).
If hypogonadism is suspected, obtain gonadotropins and sex hormone levels.
Older tests, such as TRH stimulation to evaluate hypothalamic pituitary function, are generally not needed with improved laboratory and imaging technologies.
Imaging: MRI is preferred for pituitary imaging.
It is prudent to remember that prolactin assays in large macroprolactinomas may underestimate the actual prolactin level due to the "hook effect" that results from excessive antigenic quantities.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation of the patient with elevated prolactin levels.
If a prolactinoma is found, treat medically, unless vision is imminently threatened. C
In the case of pituitary tumors that are not producing prolactin, follow guidelines such as those of the Pituitary Society. A
If hyperprolactinemia is related to drug use, attempt withdrawal of the offending medication if feasible, collaborating with treating physicians (). C
If no etiology is found, treat hyperprolactinemia medically if indicated by symptoms (eg, embarrassing galactorrhea or gonadal dysfunction). C

Treatment of hyperprolactinemia is indicated for: (1) relief of symptoms such as galactorrhea, if profuse or embarrassing; (2) restoration of normal gonadal function and fertility; and (3) prevention of bone loss likely to result from the effects of prolonged hypogonadism on bone density.
Offending medications causing hyperprolactinemia should be removed if possible.
Nonprolactin-producing pituitary tumors should be treated according to relevant guidelines specific to the type of tumor.

Most cases of prolactinomas, even large macroadenomas, can be initially treated medically unless vision is imminently threatened. Dopaminergic agents are the treatment of choice when medical treatment is chosen. Cabergoline in dosages of 0.25 to 1 mg once or twice weekly is the preferred treatment. Bromocriptine (1.25-15 mg dose range in 2-3 divided doses) is now used less frequently. Other derivatives (such as quinagolide) are not available in the United States at present.

Randomized trials have shown cabergoline to be more potent and more tolerable than bromocriptine. The option of once weekly administration may enhance compliance. Side effects include nausea, dizziness, hypotension, and headaches. First doses therefore should be the smallest available, taken at night.

Valvular heart defects have been reported with dosages exceeding 3 mg daily of cabergoline (used in the treatment of Parkinsonism). This is higher than the 0.5 mg weekly dosage typically used in hyperprolactinemia.
Studies suggest an attempt at withdrawal of medication within 2 to 5 years, and continued assessment for recurrence. Earlier withdrawal is also recommended after menopause.
In general, there is no role for surgery in prolactin-producing tumors, except for large tumors that imminently threaten vision or when medical treatment has failed.
Surgery is reserved for prolactinomas when medical treatment is intolerable or has failed.
Nonprolactinomas should be managed according to relevant guidelines.
Once treated and maintained in the normal range, hyperprolactinemia is expected to have no detrimental effects. C

There is a strong correlation between the level of prolactin and the size of prolactinomas (but not other pituitary tumors). However, the likelihood of complete clinical cure is similar for "giant" and non-giant prolactinomas.B

Incidental pituitary hemorrhage in patients with prolactinomas is 6.8% (incidence in macroprolactinomas is 20.3% vs 3.1% in microprolactinomas); most patients have complete resolution of hemmorrhage within 26 months with conservative therapy (e.g. dopamine agonist therapy). C
There is controversy regarding fetal safety and tumor enlargement in the management of prolactinomas in pregnancy.
The risk of significant tumor enlargement for prolactinomas is 1.3% and 23% for microadenomas and macroadenomas, respectively.

Although most endocrinologists stop or avoid using dopaminergic agents in pregnant women, studies have shown that women who continued to take these medications had uneventful pregnancies and healthy babies.
Medical treatment is the only option in aggressive pituitary tumors when surgery is not possible and when visual compromise is feared.
A systematic review identified only a single small trial at high risk of bias that evaluated the use of dopamine agonists in women with hyperprolactinemia to prevent recurrent miscarriage.

feature.caption: Causes of Hyperprolactinemia.
feature.feature_body:
Physiological Causes
Pregnancy
Nursing
Nipple stimulation
Sexual intercourse
Stress (surgery, hypoglycemia, myocardial infarction, syncope, trauma, venesection)
Sleep
Exercise
Food ingestion
Pharmacological Causes
Dopamine receptor antagonists
Antipsychotics
Phenothiazines
Butyrophenones
Thioxanthenes
Risperidone
Sulpiride
Antiemetics
Metoclopramide
Domperidone
Dopamine-depleting agents
a-Methyldopa
Reserpine
Antidepressants
Tricyclic antidepressants
Selective serotonin receptor inhibitors
Hormones
Estrogens (high dose)
Antiandrogens
Opiates
Verapamil
Cimetidine (IV)
Pathological Causes
Pituitary disease
Prolactinomas
Mixed GH/PRL – or ACTH/PRL-secreting adenomas
Intrasellar tumors that cause stalk compression (nonsecretory adenomas, germinoma, meningioma, glioma, metastasis)
Intrasellar cyst
Rathke's cleft cyst
Hypothalamic and pituitary stalk disease
Granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, eosinophilic granuloma)
Tumors ( craniopharyngioma, hamartoma, glioma, germinoma, metastasis)
Cranial irradiation
Pituitary stalk section
Empty sella
Vascular (aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation)
Lymphocytic hypophysitis
Others
Primary hypothyroidism
Chronic renal failure
Cirrhosis
Chest wall trauma (including surgery, herpes zoster)
Seizures
Polycystic ovarian syndrome
Ectopic secretion of prolactin (bronchogenic carcinoma, hypernephroma)
From Mah PM, Webster J. Hyperprolactinemia: etiology, diagnosis and management. Semin Reprod Med 2002;20:365-374.
